extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, theatre critics, and literary-minded readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and staging tragedy and comedy—what to show or leave offstage, how to move an audience, and when theatrical devices become ridiculous. Focused on stagecraft, moral effect, and comic artifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_children_to_move_audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "A disconsolate Mother, with a Child in her Hand, has frequently drawn Compassion from the Audience" (and writers have escalated this device: a princess with two children, later three children, and even an afflicted widow with half a dozen fatherless children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children/parent figures are powerful devices to elicit pity, but overuse or escalation (adding multiple children) turns the device from affecting to ridiculous; use sparingly and with judgment. Examples given show successive writers increasing the number of children to 'double' or 'out-write' predecessors—an anti-pattern to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: judicious_use_of_beautiful_incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus several Incidents that are beautiful in a good Writer, become ridiculous by falling into the Hands of a bad one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents or set-pieces that work in skilled hands can become absurd if mishandled or overused. Evaluate whether an incident suits the writer's ability and the play's tone; reject or use with caution when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_spectacles_of_butchery_onstage
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is none so absurd and barbarous... than that dreadful butchering of one another, which is so very frequent upon the English Stage. To delight in seeing Men stabbed, poysoned, racked, or impaled, is certainly the Sign of a cruel Temper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphic depictions of murder and torture onstage are condemned as barbarous and invite contempt. Stage designers and writers should avoid gratuitous bloodshed; frequent visible instruments of death (daggers, wheels, bowls for poison) mark a vulgar taste. Consider audience sensibilities and moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: transact_horrific_deeds_offstage
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice exemplified by Sophocles and Horace: horrific actions (parricides, unnatural murders) are better executed behind the scenes; the audience may hear cries or a dialogue and learn the fact rather than witness the deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use offstage execution when onstage depiction would be indecent or too shocking. The Sophocles example (Orestes) and Horace's lines ("Let not Medea draw her murth'ring Knife") illustrate that offstage execution, accompanied by sound or reported dialogue, can be more affecting and decorous than onstage violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: forbear_parricides_and_unnatural_murders_before_audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "By forbearing to commit Parricides or unnatural Murthers before the Audience" — Horace's rule that certain categories of murder should not be represented publicly onstage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific types of acts (parricide, extreme unnatural crimes) should not be dramatized in view of the audience; rather, have them occur offstage and be reported. This preserves decency and often increases dramatic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_offstage_dialogue_and_sounds_for_affect
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Mother is heard calling out to her Son for Mercy; and the Son answering her... there is something infinitely more affecting in this dreadful Dialogue between the Mother and her Son behind the Scenes, than could have been in anything transacted before the Audience."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ offstage voices, cries, and short reported exchanges to engage imagination and intensify emotion. Well-crafted offstage dialogue can be more moving than literal depiction onstage; consider pacing and clarity so audience understands the event's gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: produce_bodies_after_offstage_deaths
rubrics_metrics.description: "Their Bodies were often produced after their Death, which has always in it something melancholy or terrifying; so that the killing on the Stage does not seem to have been avoided only as an Indecency, but also as an Improbability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing the aftermath (a corpse presented after an offstage death) achieves melancholy or terror without depicting the act itself. Use this technique to preserve plausibility and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_unbelievable_or_cold-blooded_onstage_actions
rubrics_metrics.description: On Corneille's Horatii/Curiatii example: a hero chases his sister and refrains from killing her until they are withdrawn behind the scenes—this 'appears very unnatural, and looks like killing in cold Blood.' The author comments that the fact 'ought not to have been represented, but to have been told.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an onstage action reads as implausible or emotionally inconsistent (e.g., delayed killing that looks like cold-bloodedness), prefer narration or offstage handling. Maintain psychological credibility of characters and avoid staging that makes motives seem artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: allow_greater_latitude_in_comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Because Ridicule is not so delicate as Compassion... there is a much greater Latitude for comick than tragick Artifices, and by Consequence a much greater Indulgence to be allowed them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy can rely on broader, cruder, or more overt devices (costume, props, physical jests) than tragedy. Writers may exploit visual gags, exaggerated dress, and stock physical traits (broad vs narrow-brimmed hats, a lover peeping out of a barrel, shoulder-belts, whiskers) more freely, but still with attention to taste and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_forceful_imitation_of_natural_behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: "A natural and unconstrained Behaviour has something in it so agreeable... but... it is so very hard to hit, when it is not Born with us, that People often make themselves Ridiculous in attempting it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efforts to manufacture 'natural' or unconstrained behavior (coquetry affected as refined manners) often fall flat and become ridiculous. Prioritize genuine character and credible manner; do not contrive spontaneity that the actor/writer cannot deliver.
